```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(knowledgelayer)
root <- file.path(tempdir(), "example-city")
unlink(root, recursive = TRUE)
```

Two analysts in the same office describe the same work in different words.
One registers a "vendor payments extract", the other a "contracting
review". A search for either finds only one. A **shared vocabulary** fixes
that: both are tagged with the same concept, and a search for any of its
names finds both.

This vignette follows the inspector general's office of Example City, an
invented city with invented program areas, as it starts using the
vocabulary that ships with the package.

## What ships

```{r}
kl_init(root)
v <- kl_vocab(path = root)
table(v$scheme)
```

Each concept has a short id, a preferred label and alternative labels: the
abbreviations, older names and everyday words people actually use. The
short ids are the stable identifiers. Tags store them, never a web address.

```{r}
ft <- kl_vocab("findings_typology", path = root)
head(ft[, c("id", "prefLabel")], 8)
```

## From free text to a concept

`kl_resolve()` matches a term against every label, ignoring case and extra
spaces. It never guesses. A term that matches nothing is reported as
`"no concept"`, and a term that matches more than one concept is reported as
`"ambiguous"`, with the candidates.

```{r}
r <- kl_resolve(c("separation of duties", "embezzlement", "snow plowing"), path = root)
r[, c("term", "status", "id", "candidates")]
```

"Embezzlement" is a synonym both of fraud as an oversight concept and of
fraud as a kind of finding. Say which scheme you mean:

```{r}
kl_resolve("embezzlement", scheme = "findings_typology", path = root)$id
```

## Example City's own program areas

Every office has program areas, and they are its own. The vocabulary ships
nine broad clusters and a set of common program areas under them. They are
starters: meant to be broadly applicable, but they may not fit every
office perfectly. Some, such as Medicaid or TANF, are typically run by
states or counties, and an office that does not oversee them can ignore
them. Look at what is there before adding anything:

```{r}
pa <- kl_vocab("program_areas", path = root)
nrow(pa)
head(pa[pa$broader == "cluster:infrastructure", c("id", "prefLabel")])
```

Example City keeps its own areas in a spreadsheet, each one placed under a
cluster or under another area:

```{r}
csv <- file.path(tempdir(), "example-city-areas.csv")
writeLines(c(
  "id,prefLabel,altLabels,broader",
  "area:snow,Snow and Ice Control,snow plowing; road salting,cluster:infrastructure",
  "area:bridges,Bridge Inspection,bridge maintenance,cluster:infrastructure",
  "area:harbor,Harbor Authority Operations,harbor; port operations,cluster:economic-development",
  "area:meals,Senior Meals Program,meals on wheels,cluster:human-services"
), csv)
kl_vocab_import(csv, path = root)
```

The import checks every row before it writes any: if one area points at a
`broader` that does not exist, nothing is imported. The result is the
vocabulary check, run on the shipped set and the office's terms together.
The warnings are labels shared by two schemes on purpose, such as "audit"
the activity and "audit" the report.

The areas are kept in `knowledge/vocabulary.json`, beside the shipped
vocabulary and never written into it. Single terms are added the same way:

```{r}
kl_vocab_extend("agencies", "agency:streets", "Example City Department of Streets",
                altLabels = c("Streets", "DoS"), path = root)
kl_resolve("snow plowing", path = root)$id
```

## Tagging the work

```{r}
kl_add_project("snow-2026", "Winter road treatment review", owner = "Analyst A",
               sources = "Fleet GPS logs", concepts = c("snow and ice control", "contracting"),
               path = root)
kl_add_project("vendors-2026", "Vendor payments extract", owner = "Analyst B",
               sources = "Accounts payable", path = root)
kl_tag("project", "vendors-2026", c("procurement and contracting", "duplicate payment"), path = root)
kl_find("contracting", path = root)[, c("id", "title")]
```

Neither project mentions "contracting" in its own words, and both are found.

## Findings carry their kind

A finding's `typology` says what kind of deficiency it is. The review page
then shows the kind and its crosswalks to the standards it relates to, each
labeled with how precise its link is.

```{r}
f <- kl_findings(
  id = c("F1", "F2"),
  finding = c("The same clerk enters and approves salt purchase orders",
              "Two plow contracts were paid twice in February"),
  severity = c("high", "high"),
  proposed_fix = c("Separate entry and approval", "Recover the duplicate payments"),
  typology = c("segregation of duties", "improper payment"), path = root)
f[, c("id", "typology")]
```

On its own, "improper payment" is ambiguous: it is also the name of a
program area. Here the context settles it, because a finding's kind can
only come from the findings typology. `kl_resolve()` with no context still
declines to choose, and lists both.

A link that goes to an exact principle says so. A link to a whole standard
says "link to the whole standard, not to this point", so nobody mistakes a
general citation for a precise one.

## Exporting as SKOS

To load the vocabulary into a linked-data tool, export it as Turtle.
The package does not choose a web address for the concepts: you supply
`base`, and there is no default.

```{r}
ttl <- file.path(tempdir(), "example-city.ttl")
kl_export_skos(ttl, base = "https://data.example.org/vocab/", projects = TRUE, path = root)
cat(readLines(ttl)[grep("area/snow> a", readLines(ttl)) + 0:4], sep = "\n")
```
